abstract: Cu-based materials are promising electrocatalysts for the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). However, they still suffer from intense hydrogen evolution, as well as low selectivity and efficiency for the CO2RR. In this work, Cu–In bimetallic catalysts for the CO2RR were prepared by the pyrolysis of Cu–In metal–organic framework (MOF) materials. Cu90In10/C with a Cu/In molar ratio of 9/1 exhibited a high CO selectivity of up to 85% at −0.75 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, compared with 3.1% on Cu/C and 10.8% on In/ C. On the Cu90In10/C catalyst, In was found to be locally distributed on the surface of Cu nanoparticles, forming Cu4In, changing the geometric and electronic structures of the Cu surface. These modifications were supposed to have modulated the adsorption properties of the catalyst for *H, CO2 and the intermediates during the CO2RR, therefore the electrochemical conversion of CO2 to CO was enhanced and hydrogen evolution was mitigated. The enlarged electrochemically active surface area and the accelerated charge transfer and reaction kinetics of this Cu–In bimetallic catalyst also contributed much to its excellent CO2RR performance. This work not only highlights the superior CO2 electroreduction performance of bimetals over monometals, but also provides a new method to develop bimetallic catalysts.

Cu-based materials are promising electrocatalysts for the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). However, they still suffer from intense hydrogen evolution, as well as low selectivity and efficiency for the CO2RR. In this work, Cu–In bimetallic catalysts for the CO2RR were prepared by the pyrolysis of Cu–In metal–organic framework (MOF) materials. Cu90In10/C with a Cu/In molar ratio of 9/1 exhibited a high CO selectivity of up to 85% at −0.75 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, compared with 3.1% on Cu/C and 10.8% on In/ C. On the Cu90In10/C catalyst, In was found to be locally distributed on the surface of Cu nanoparticles, forming Cu4In, changing the geometric and electronic structures of the Cu surface. These modifications were supposed to have modulated the adsorption properties of the catalyst for *H, CO2 and the intermediates during the CO2RR, therefore the electrochemical conversion of CO2 to CO was enhanced and hydrogen evolution was mitigated. The enlarged electrochemically active surface area and the
accelerated charge transfer and reaction kinetics of this Cu–In bimetallic catalyst also contributed much to
its excellent CO2RR performance. This work not only highlights the superior CO2 electroreduction performance of bimetals over monometals, but also provides a new method to develop bimetallic catalysts.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
The consumption of fossil fuels has brought about climate issues such as global warming due to the excessive emission of CO2. In order to alleviate environmental pressure and realize a carbon-neutral cycle, it is of great significance to develop sustainable approaches for CO2 conversion.
1 By electrochemical reduction under mild conditions with renewable electricity from solar, wind, tide, etc., CO2 can be converted to highly valuable chemicals and fuels, such as CO, HCOOH, CH4, ethanol and other hydrocarbons,
2–4 which are feedstocks of chemical industries. To meet the criteria for practical applications, the research on CO2 electrochemical reduction mainly focuses on pursuing high product faradaic efficiency (FE) and CO2-conversion efficiency.
5 However, the efficiency of the CO2RR is still very low, because of the high
overvoltage to produce various carbon-containing chemicals and the competition between the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at the cathode.6–8 Therefore, it is urgent to develop efficient catalysts to boost the CO2RR and effectively inhibit the HER.
Multifarious metal catalysts have been applied in the CO2RR, such as Pd, Au, Ag, and Cu.9 Among them, Cu, as one of the non-noble metals, can electrochemically reduce CO2 to various products, including C1, C2 and even long-chain chemicals, at modest overpotentials.10,11 Unfortunately, Cu shows poor selectivity to single products because of the multiple proton–electron coupled transfer pathways of the CO2RR on it.
12 Furthermore, because the edge-site Cu atoms prefer to adsorb protons,13 single metal Cu tends to show intense activity for the HER rather than for the CO2RR. In order to improve the CO2RR activity and the product selectivity on Cu-based catalysts, many modification strategies have been reported, such as oxide-derivative preparation,14 hetero-element doping,15 and size and morphology regulation.16,17 Coupling Cu with another metal is an effective way to change the pathway of the CO2RR and improve the FE of a specific product by optimizing the surface adsorption energy of intermediates.18,19 For instance, Mun et al.20 synthesized Cu–Pd bimetallic nanoparticles, which had low affinity for *H and suppressed the protonation of CO. As a result, the CO selectivity on this

catalyst was up to 89%. However, considering the high cost of noble metals, it is more feasible to couple Cu with other non-precious metals to improve the CO2RR activity.
Post-transition metals, such as In, Sn, and Bi, have low affinity towards *H and high overpotentials for the HER,21,22 and are regarded as promising catalysts to enhance the CO2RR and mitigate the HER. However, they show weak adsorption ability towards CO2 and intermediates in the CO2RR,23 which leads to low activity and slow kinetics for the CO2RR. Through alloying Cu with post-transition metals, the binding energy of CO2 and intermediates (*COOH, *OCHO, *H, etc.) can be modulated by tuning the local electronic and/ or geometric structures, and the activity of Cu-based catalysts in the CO2RR can be further boosted.
20,24 For example, Cu– Sn alloy nanoparticles achieved 93% selectivity to C1 products (HCOOH and CO account for 53% and 40%, respectively) at −1.0 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE),25 which was considerably higher than that on the single Cu and Sn counterparts. However, the selectivity to a target product was still low. Cu–In alloy materials were synthesized and ran into the same problem: the selectivity to CO was only 63%.19 Therefore, it is highly desired to develop new bimetallic catalysts to promote the selectivity to a single target product.
Considering that metal–organic framework (MOF) derived carbon materials are promising electrochemical catalysts for the CO2RR due to their ultra-high porosity, high conductivity, and excellent CO2 adsorption ability,
26,27 herein, we synthesized bimetallic electrocatalysts with different Cu/In atomic ratios by pyrolyzing MOF precursors. And their CO2 electrochemical performances were investigated in 0.1 M KHCO3 using a three-electrode cell. It was found that the Cu– In bimetallic nanocatalyst with an atomic content of 90% Cu and 10% In exhibited a maximum FECO of about 85%, which was almost 7.9 and 26.9 times higher than that on single In/ C and Cu/C, respectively. The synergistic effect between Cu and In changed the surface electronic and geometric structures of the bimetallic nanoparticles, which tuned the adsorption energy of *H, CO2 and the intermediates during the CO2RR, leading to high selectivity to CO.

sections.heading: 2.1 Materials
sections.text: 1,3,5-Benzenetricarboxylic acid (H3BTC), copper(II) nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO)3·3H2O), indium(III) nitrate hydrate (In(NO3)3·xH2O), potassium hydrogen carbonate (KHCO3), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and isopropyl alcohol were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. All the reagents were used as received. Glassy carbon, Ag/AgCl and Pt plate electrodes were obtained from Aida Corporation, Tianjin.

sections.heading: 2.2 Preparation of catalysts
sections.text:
CuxIn100−x MOFs: CuxIn100−x MOFs (x is the molar percentage of Cu in the precursors) were synthesized by a hydrothermal procedure. 5 mmol of H3BTC was dissolved in 50 mL of a mixed
solvent of ethanol and deionized water (volume ratio = 1 : 1). Then Cu(NO)3·3H2O and In(NO3)3·xH2O with different molar ratios were ultrasonically dissolved in the above solution, followed by stirring for 30 min at room temperature to form a homogeneous solution. The solution was heated at 85 °C under constant stirring for 6 h, and then transferred to a Teflon-lined autoclave and kept at 120 °C for 12 h. After centrifugation and washing with ethanol and water several times, CuxIn100−x MOFs were collected and dried at 60 °C under vacuum. Cu or In MOFs were also synthesized with the same procedure without adding In(NO3)3·xH2O or Cu(NO)3·3H2O, respectively.
Carbon supported Cu–In bimetallic catalysts (CuxIn100−x/ C): 0.5 g of the as-prepared CuxIn100−x MOF powder was calcined in a tube furnace at 900 °C for 2 h under an Ar atmosphere with a ramp rate of 5 °C min−1. Cu/C or In/C was synthesized with the same method. The whole scheme of the preparation of CuxIn100−x/C catalysts is shown in Scheme 1.

sections.heading: 2.3 Characterization
sections.text: A Rigaku D/Max 2200PC X-ray diffractometer was used to obtain the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns with a scanning rate of 4° min−1 at an acceleration voltage of 40 kV and applied current of 40 mA at room temperature. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) were carried out on a field-emission JEM2010 microscope at 200 kV. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were collected on a Hitachi S-4800 microscope. A Micromeritics 3020 system was used to measure the N2 adsorption–desorption isotherms at 77 K. The surface area of the catalysts was calculated by the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) method and the pore size distribution (PSD) was calculated by the Barrett–Joyner–Halenda (BJH) method. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Auger electron spectroscopy (AES) were performed on a Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250 spectrometer with an Al Kα radiation source (1486.6 eV), and Ar ion etching was performed with an acceleration voltage of 2 kV for 10 s to characterize the chemical states and element contents on the subsurface. The binding energy was calibrated with C 1s at 284.8 eV. The bulk Cu/In atomic ratio was measured using an inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES, Agilent 5100) with 0.5 g of samples.

Electrochemical reduction of CO2: electroreduction experiments were performed on a VSP electrochemical workstation (Bio-Logic, Germany) using a cell with two compartments separated by an N117 membrane (DuPont) at room temperature. The counter and reference electrodes were a Pt plate (10 × 10 × 0.2 mm) and a Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl), respectively. 30 mL of 0.1 M KHCO3 solution, poured into each part of the cells, was used as the electrolyte, which was bubbled with CO2 for 30 min to reach saturation (pH 6.8) at the beginning of each measurement. Before each potentiostatic test, linear sweep voltammetric (LSV) curves were swept four times to activate the catalysts. The reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) potentials were converted based on the following equation: ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.21 + 0.0591 × pH. All potentials cited in this paper were versus RHE unless stated otherwise.

sections.heading: 2.5 Product analysis
sections.text: The gas products (CO, CH4) were analyzed using an offline gas chromatograph (Shimadzu, GC-2014) equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID). H2 was analyzed using a gas chromatograph (Techcomp, GC7900) equipped with a thermal conductive detector (TCD) and a 5 Å molecular sieve column. Both GCs used N2 as carrier gas. The gas products were sampled by extracting 1 mL of the gas at the cathode in an H-cell after each potentiostatic test with a gas injector, and then injected to GC for analysis. The liquid products were analyzed using a nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer (NMR, 500 MHz, Bruker) with water suppression. The solution used for 1H NMR analysis was mixed with 500 μL of electrolyte after the electrochemical reduction test and 100 μL of D2O containing 0.78 μmol of DMSO which was used as the internal standard.

sections.heading: 3.1 CO2 electroreduction performance
sections.text:
The CO2RR activity on CuxIn100−x/C catalysts was tested at room temperature in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. For consistency, the linear sweep voltammetric (LSV) curves at the fourth cycle of all the catalysts were used and are shown in Fig. 1a and S1a.† The current density measured in Arsaturated electrolyte corresponds to the HER28 which is a competition reaction of the CO2RR at the cathode, while the current density under CO2-saturated conditions corresponds to the sum of the HER and CO2RR.
29 Notably, the current densities acquired on the as-obtained samples in CO2saturated electrolyte are all higher than those under Arsaturated conditions, indicating that they all show CO2RR catalytic performance.30,31 Among them, In/C shows the lowest current density under CO2-purged condition, which may arise from the poor conductivity of In and its excellent
performance in inhibiting hydrogen evolution.32 Cu/C shows the highest current density in CO2-saturated electrolyte; however, there is little difference between its current densities in Ar- and CO2-saturated electrolytes, revealing the more intense HER than the CO2RR on Cu/C. For Cu10In90/C, Cu50In50/C and Cu90In10/C, the current density under CO2saturated conditions becomes higher with more Cu added (Fig. 1a and S1a†), which may arise from the gradually elevated CO2RR activity on them. Among these three catalysts, Cu90In10/C exhibits the highest current density under CO2-saturated conditions, as well as the largest variance between the current densities in Ar- and CO2saturated electrolytes, reflecting its superior activity in the CO2RR to that in the HER.
CO, HCOOH and H2 were detected as the products and their Faradaic efficiency (FE) on the catalysts was calculated. It is noted that the FE of H2 (FEH2) on Cu/C reaches above 50%, which is much higher than the FECO and FEHCOOOH over all the applied potentials (Fig. 1c), indicating that the HER is more favorable on Cu/C, agreeing well with the results of LSV. On In/C (Fig. 1d), FECO is below 10% over all the applied potentials, while FEHCOOH increases from 5% at −0.7 V to 39% at −0.9 V, which is consistent with the previous CO2RR reports that CO2 could be electrochemically reduced to HCOOH by In catalysts.33 Besides, compared with Cu/C, In/C shows decreased FEH2 to about 30%, indicating that the HER has been mitigated, which is believed to originate from the high hydrogen evolution overpotential on In.34 However, the selectivity to a single product of the CO2RR is poor on In/ C. Both CO and HCOOH are produced on Cu10In90/C, Cu50In50/C and Cu90In10/C, and FECO becomes higher with the increase of the Cu content (Fig. S1d†). Cu90In10/C exhibits remarkably improved selectivity to CO (Fig. 1b). As the applied potential increases, the selectivity to CO on Cu90In10/ C shows a volcanic trend and reaches a maximum of about

The partial current densities of CO over the applied potentials on Cu90In10/C are all higher than those on Cu/C and In/C (Fig. S2a†), indicating its high CO2RR activity. The FEH2 on Cu90In10/C has been inhibited below 20%, which may be related to the synergistic effect between Cu and In. sections.heading: 3.2 Structure and composition of the catalysts
sections.text:
The structure and composition of the as-obtained catalysts were further characterized by XRD. As shown in Fig. 2a, the crystal structures of the Cu MOF and In MOF are consistent with previous reports,35,36 and the Cu90In10 MOF shows characteristic peaks of both the Cu-MOF and In-MOF, indicating that the Cu90In10 MOF precursor has been successfully prepared. CuxIn100−x/C samples were obtained by pyrolyzing CuxIn100−x MOFs at high temperature. As shown in Fig. 2b, the crystal phase composition of In/C is mainly metallic In (JCPDS card No. 05-0642), accompanied by a small amount of In2O3 (JCPDS card No. 06-0416) caused by the surface oxidation of In. Cu/C shows strong characteristic peaks at 43.3°, 50.4° and 74.1°, corresponding to metallic Cu (JCPDS card No. 04-0836). Besides metal In and In2O3, Cu10In90/C and Cu50In50/C exhibit characteristic peaks centred at 29.4, 41.4 and 42.3, corresponding to Cu11In9 (JCPDS card No. 41-0883), and no Cu species was detected (Fig. S4†). Cu90In10/C, with a high content of Cu, shows the crystal phase of metallic Cu, In2O3 and Cu4In (JCPDS card No. 42-1477) which can be identified by the characteristic peaks at 42.6°, 61.9° and 78.1°. The transformation from Cu11In9 in Cu10In90/C and Cu50In50/C to Cu4In in Cu90In10/C is considered to be related to the Cu/In molar ratio in the precursor.
SEM and TEM were used to further characterize the morphology and composition of the catalysts. According to previous reports, Cu and In MOFs exhibited octahedral and
nanorod-like morphologies, respectively.35,36 Containing both Cu MOF and In MOF, the Cu90In10 MOF precursor shows an adhesion morphology of octahedra and nanorods (Fig. 3a). By the pyrolysis of the MOF precursors, CuxIn100−x/C preserves the morphologies of the MOFs. As can be seen in Fig. S5a and b,† Cu/C is octahedral, in which there are some nanoparticles identified as Cu nanoparticles. In/C exhibits a nanorod morphology with some micropores rather than nanoparticles on the surface (Fig. S5c and d†). Cu90In10/C retains the adhesion morphology of octahedra and nanorods of the Cu90In10 MOF with a mass of irregular nanoparticles distributed on the surface, and the size of the nanoparticles is about 200–400 nm (Fig. 3b and c). TEM and EDS were used to further characterize the composition of the nanoparticles. As shown in Fig. 3d–g, the EDS elemental mapping images show that the nanoparticles consist of both Cu and In, that is, these nanoparticles are Cu–In bimetals. Meanwhile, the element O mainly coexists with the element C. Only a small amount of O is distributed on the bimetallic nanoparticles, which may originate from the surface oxidation of the metals.
The chemical states of the metals on the catalyst surface were characterized by XPS and AES. In Fig. 4a, the Cu 2p XPS spectra of Cu/C and Cu90In10/C show the peaks of Cu 2p3/2 at about 932.8 and 934.8 eV corresponding to Cu+/Cu0 and Cu2+, respectively.37 The AES spectra in Fig. 4b present two characteristic peaks at 568.6 e and 570.5 eV assigned to Cu0 and Cu+, respectively.38 It can be concluded that on the surface of Cu/C and Cu90In10/C, Cu is in the multivalent state of 0, +1 and +2. After etching by Ar ions for 10 s, the satellite peaks of Cu2+ on the subsurface of Cu/C and Cu90In10/C disappear (Fig. S7a and b†), indicating that the Cu2+ on the surface is derived from surface oxidation in air. The In 3d XPS spectrum of In/C shows two characteristic peaks at 445.2 and 452.8 eV relative to In 3d5/2 and In 3d3/2 of In
3+, respectively (Fig. 4c),33 which may be induced by the surface oxidation of In in air.39 The In 3d binding energy values of Cu90In10/C negatively shift compared with those of In/C (Fig. 4c). Meanwhile, the Cu 2p binding energy values of Cu90In10/C positively shift compared with those of Cu/C (Fig. S7c†). Based on these results, the electron transfer from Cu to In has happened, resulting in electronic richness of In,

that is, the surface electronic structure of the Cu catalysts has been modified by the In introduction.40 Considering that the critical step of the CO2RR (CO2 + e − → *CO2 −) involves an electron transfer to CO2, for Cu90In10/C, the modification of its surface electronic structure is beneficial to improving the reaction rate of this bottleneck step and modulating the adsorption energy of the intermediates,41 thus improving its CO2RR activity.
Ar ion etching was applied to further analyze the content of Cu and In on the subsurface of Cu90In10/C (Fig. 4d). Before etching, the Cu/In atomic ratio is 3.78, close to the atomic ratio of Cu4In shown by XRD. After etching, the Cu/In atomic ratio increases to 6.24, while the actual bulk Cu/In atomic ratio measured by ICP-OES is 11.07 (Table S1†), indicating that the content of Cu on the subsurface is higher than that on the surface. It can be deduced that in Cu90In10/C particles, Cu4In is mainly distributed on the surface while Cu mainly exists inside the particles, which may be caused by the relatively low melting point and low content of In. The specific geometric structure of Cu90In10/C may optimize the binding strength of *H and *COOH,19 further increasing the selectivity to CO.

sections.heading: 3.3 Mechanism analysis
sections.text:
As mentioned above, Cu90In10/C exhibits the highest selectivity to CO, indicating its enhanced CO2RR activity. But the specific surface area of In/C, Cu10In90/C, Cu50In50/C, Cu90In10/C and Cu/C acquired by the BET method is 259.8, 184.5, 156.4, 191.4 and 147.7 cm3 g−1, respectively (Fig. S9†), which is not consistent with their CO2RR performance. Therefore, surface area is not the key contributor to the CO2RR performance of these catalysts.
To explore the intrinsic activity, electrochemical characterization was performed and analyzed. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves were tested in a non-faradaic
potential range with different scan rates (Fig. S10†), and the charging current density differences between the anode and cathode voltages of the CV curves were plotted against the scan rates and are shown in Fig. 5a and S10f.† The doublelayer capacitance (Cdl) values, which are half of the slopes, of these catalysts are in the order of Cu90In10/C > Cu50In50/C > Cu10In90/C > Cu/C > In/C, suggesting that Cu90In10/C exhibits the largest electrochemically active surface area (ECSA), due to the positive relationship of ECSA and Cdl. 42 Therefore, for Cu90In10/C, the highest catalytic activity is favored by the most active sites, which may be related to Cu4In species distributed on the Cu surface.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of the catalysts was conducted at open circuit potential (Fig. 5b and S11b†). Among the as-obtained catalysts, the impedance radius of Cu90In10/C is the smallest, indicating that Cu90In10/ C has the lowest charge-transfer resistance (Rct) and fastest electron-transfer rate,43 which accelerated the reaction rate of the CO2 reduction to CO. It is inferred that the lowest impedance is caused by the electronic effect between Cu and In, which accelerates the electron transfer from the catalyst to CO2.
Based on previous reports,28 the reaction pathways of the CO2 electrocatalytic reduction to CO are as follows:
CO2(aq) + e − → *CO2 −(aq) (1)
*CO2 −(aq) + H+ → *COOH(aq) (2)
*COOH(aq) + H+ + e− → *CO(aq) + H2O (3)
*CO(aq) → CO(g) (4)
where * represents the active site on the catalyst surface where the intermediate can be bonded to. The Tafel slope is

generally used to evaluate the kinetics of the electrocatalytic reaction. To obtain the Tafel slopes, electrochemical reactions have been carried out in the low overpotential region, where the CO2RR was kinetically controlled. As shown in Fig. 5c and S11a,† the Tafel slopes of Cu90In10/C, Cu50In50/ C, Cu10In90/C, Cu/C and In/C are 147.4, 178.2, 183.7, 254.9, and 230.1 mV dec−1, respectively, which are close to 118 mV dec−1, indicating that the rate-determining step of the CO2RR on these catalysts is step (1):30 the formation of the CO2 − intermediate from CO2 by accepting an electron. Moreover, the Tafel slope value of Cu90In10/C is the smallest among these materials, indicating its fastest reaction kinetics, thus boosting its highest activity for the CO2RR. Hence, the electronic structure of Cu90In10/C favors the reaction kinetics and activity for the CO2RR.
As is known, the activity of Cu-based catalysts for CO2 conversion is strongly related to their chemical state, morphology, crystal facet, etc.44–46 For example, oxide derived-Cu materials have been reported to be effective in improving CO selectivity, which may arise from their electronically unsaturated sites.44,47 Through crystal facet engineering, the specific facet of Cu could be exposed to obtain high CO selectivity. By DFT calculation, Cao and coworkers46 demonstrated that the Gibbs free energy required for *COOH formation on Cu (110) is much lower than that on Cu (111), indicating that Cu (110) is more active for CO formation than the (111) facet. However, in the Cu/C catalyst in this work, the main phase is metallic Cu rather than CuxO. And the main facet of Cu is (111), as indicated by the diffraction peak at 43.3° in the XRD pattern. These two factors may induce its low CO selectivity.
By coupling Cu with In, the pathway of the CO2RR may have been changed by optimizing the surface adsorption energy of the intermediates, thus improving the selectivity to CO. It has been proved that Cu atoms on edge sites are active for *H adsorption,13 thus, Cu catalysts exhibit high hydrogen evolution activity. Meanwhile, In atoms exhibit low adsorption energy for *H, indicating that In catalysts are potential candidates for the CO2RR,
34 Moreover, Cu atoms on edge sites prefer to be replaced by In atoms,19 therefore the HER can be slowed down.32 Considering that the catalytic reactions mainly happen on the surface of materials,48,49 in this work, the introduction of In has modified the geometric structure of Cu90In10/C by forming Cu4In on the surface of Cu, thus weakening *H adsorption and inhibiting the HER. Such a specific geometric structure of Cu90In10/C may also optimize the binding strength of *COOH,19 further increasing the selectivity to CO. And the optimized electronic structure arising from the electron transfer between Cu and In is favorable for enhancing the CO2 adsorption on the catalysts, further facilitating CO2 transformation to carboncontaining intermediates.40 On the other hand, the adsorption energies of *COOH and CO on Cu are −1.5 eV and −0.7 eV, while those on In are −1.0 eV and 0 eV, respectively,49 reflecting the more convenient desorption of CO from In. It can be concluded that the presence of In may
not only improve the stability of *COOH, but also benefit the desorption of CO.41,50 Besides, because of the low adsorption of *H, CO-targeting intermediates are difficult to be further hydrogenated. As a result, CO, as the main end-product, is ready to desorb from the surface of Cu90In10/C.
Conclusions
In summary, a carbon supported Cu–In bimetallic catalyst was synthesized by pyrolyzing CuIn-MOF precursors. Compared with the counterpart catalysts of single Cu and monometallic In, the Cu–In bimetallic catalyst with a Cu/In mole ratio of 9/1 showed remarkably enhanced CO selectivity in the CO2RR, which reached about 85% at −0.75 V vs. RHE. Cu4In was formed on the surface and the electron transfer from Cu to In locally modified the geometric and electronic structures of the Cu-based catalyst, thus optimizing the adsorption of *H, CO2 and the intermediates (e.g., *COOH) during the CO2RR, tuning the reaction pathway of the CO2RR and improving the selectivity to CO. The electrochemically active surface area of the bimetal catalyst was enlarged compared with that of the monometallic Cu and In counterparts. And the synthesized Cu–In bimetallic catalyst also exhibited lowered electron transfer impedance and an accelerated electron transfer rate and reaction kinetics, leading to its enhanced CO2RR activity. This work not only provides a new strategy to fabricate Cu–In bimetallic electrocatalysts for the CO2RR, but also gives an example to modify the surface structure of Cu-based catalysts to enhance their CO2RR activity and selectivity.

There are no conflicts to declare.
